name: Ginger
oneLineAnswer: A common spice and supplement, studied mostly for nausea, with results that vary by cause.
whatItDoes: Ginger is the underground stem, called a rhizome, of the plant Zingiber officinale.
The plant comes from warm parts of Asia and is now grown in Africa and South America too.
People have used it as a folk remedy since ancient times, often for stomach problems and flu.
Today it is sold mostly for nausea and vomiting, menstrual cramps, and knee arthritis.
Studies suggest it may help pregnancy nausea, but most studies found no help for motion sickness.
whatWeDoNotKnow: Whether ginger adds anything to standard treatment for chemotherapy or surgery nausea is still uncertain.
Knee arthritis trials exist, but much of that research was poor quality, so its results are hard to trust.
No one knows whether ginger is safe to use while breastfeeding.
The sources read here do not explain how ginger might work in the body.
Ginger labels in the FDA database are mostly mixtures or skin products, not evidence of benefit.
gaps: No FDA-approved drug label for ginger as a single-ingredient medicine was found. Every ginger-containing label returned by openFDA was a homeopathic combination (A-29, HAD) or a topical cosmetic-type product (nail and scalp oils), so none of them states a ginger indication.
NCCIH's page describes what has been studied but not a mechanism, so this record explains no biology of action beyond the plant part used.

The NCCIH page renders through JavaScript. A plain fetch returned only page code, so the page text was read through a browser render instead. Two subsequent plain fetches returned no matching passages.
A DailyMed search for ginger returned only product titles with no descriptive text, and a PubChem lookup for 'ginger oil' returned HTTP 404.
No long-term safety information was found. NCCIH reports safe use within research studies but gives no duration.
No information was found on how much of any ginger compound reaches the bloodstream, or on which compound would matter. This record therefore states no dose and no personal protocol.

evidence.claim: Ginger is the rhizome, an underground stem, of the plant Zingiber officinale, used both as food and for health purposes.
evidence.quote: Its rhizome (underground stem) is used in food and for health purposes.

evidence.claim: Ginger is native to warm parts of Asia and is now grown in South America, Africa, and the Middle East.
evidence.quote: Ginger is native to the warm parts of Asia and is now grown in parts of South America, Africa, and the Middle East.

evidence.claim: Ginger has been used in folk medicine since ancient times, traditionally for conditions such as asthma, flu, indigestion, and gastrointestinal discomfort.
evidence.quote: It was traditionally used for a variety of conditions such as asthma, flu, indigestion, and gastrointestinal discomfort.

evidence.claim: Ginger is currently promoted for nausea and vomiting, osteoarthritis, and menstrual cramps.
evidence.quote: Ginger is currently promoted for nausea and vomiting, osteoarthritis, menstrual cramps, and other conditions.

evidence.claim: Many human studies of ginger exist, but some were not high quality.
evidence.quote: There have been many studies on the use of ginger for health purposes in people, but some of them have not been of high quality.

evidence.claim: Most studies of ginger tested dietary supplements rather than ginger-containing foods.
evidence.quote: Most of the studies tested dietary supplements rather than foods.

evidence.claim: Research shows ginger may be helpful for nausea and vomiting during pregnancy.
evidence.quote: Research shows that ginger may be helpful for nausea and vomiting associated with pregnancy.

evidence.claim: Most studies of ginger for motion sickness have not shown it to be helpful.
evidence.quote: Most studies of ginger for motion sickness haven’t shown it to be helpful.

evidence.claim: It is uncertain whether ginger helps as an addition to standard treatment for chemotherapy-related nausea and vomiting.
evidence.quote: It’s uncertain whether ginger is a helpful addition to standard treatments for nausea and vomiting associated with cancer chemotherapy

evidence.claim: It is also uncertain whether ginger helps with nausea and vomiting after surgery.
evidence.quote: and whether it’s helpful for nausea and vomiting after surgery.

evidence.claim: Ginger dietary supplements might help reduce the severity of menstrual cramps.
evidence.quote: Research suggests that ginger dietary supplements might be helpful for reducing the severity of menstrual cramps.

evidence.claim: Ginger dietary supplements might help knee osteoarthritis symptoms, but much of the research was poor quality.
evidence.quote: Ginger dietary supplements might be helpful for symptoms of knee osteoarthritis, but much of the research has been of poor quality.

evidence.claim: Ginger applied to the skin has not been shown to help knee osteoarthritis symptoms.
evidence.quote: Ginger used topically (applied to the skin) has not been shown to be helpful for knee osteoarthritis symptoms.

evidence.claim: Oral ginger has been used safely in many research studies, and ginger products may also be safe for topical use.
evidence.quote: Ginger has been used safely in many research studies where it was taken orally (by mouth) as a dietary supplement.

evidence.claim: Side effects of oral ginger can include abdominal discomfort, heartburn, diarrhea, and mouth and throat irritation.
evidence.quote: Ginger can have side effects such as abdominal discomfort, heartburn, diarrhea, and mouth and throat irritation when taken orally.

evidence.claim: NCCIH advises anyone taking any type of medicine to talk with a health care provider before using ginger.
evidence.quote: If you take any type of medicine, talk with your health care provider before using ginger or any other herbal products

evidence.claim: Little is known about whether ginger is safe to use while breastfeeding.
evidence.quote: Little is known about whether it’s safe to use ginger while breastfeeding.

evidence.claim: Ginger supplements sold as dietary supplements are not approved by the FDA before sale, unlike drugs.
evidence.quote: Unlike drugs, dietary supplements are not approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) before they are sold to the public.

evidence.claim: NCCIH states its ginger publication is not copyrighted and is in the public domain.
evidence.quote: This publication is not copyrighted and is in the public domain. Duplication is encouraged.

evidence.claim: MedlinePlus lists ginger under treatments and therapies on its federal health topic page for nausea and vomiting.
evidence.quote: Ginger (National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health)

evidence.claim: The ClinicalTrials.gov registry returns 297 studies for the search term ginger.
evidence.quote: "totalCount": 297

evidence.claim: Registered ginger studies include a completed trial of ginger capsules for migraine prevention.
evidence.quote: Ginger Capsules for the Prophylactic Treatment of Migraine

evidence.claim: Registered ginger studies include a completed trial comparing ginger extract with loratadine for allergic rhinitis.
evidence.quote: Study of Efficacy and Safety of Ginger Extract Compared With Loratadine for Treatment of Allergic Rhinitis

evidence.claim: PubChem records 6-gingerol, a compound found in ginger, with the molecular formula C17H26O4.
evidence.quote: "MolecularFormula": "C17H26O4"

evidence.claim: PubChem gives 6-gingerol a molecular weight of 294.4.
evidence.quote: "MolecularWeight": "294.4"

evidence.claim: A registered homeopathic over-the-counter product label lists Zingiber officinale (Ginger) Rhizome as an active ingredient.
evidence.quote: Zingiber officinale (Ginger) Rhizome 2X

evidence.claim: Ginger root oil is a labeled active ingredient in some topical over-the-counter products in the FDA label database.
evidence.quote: ZINGIBER OFFICINALE (GINGER) ROOT OIL
